Part 1 asks what a claim in social science is for, why people describe the field as being in crisis, how three very large studies measured the problem, and what a computational toolchain has to do with any of it. The part takes ninety minutes. The hands-on work comes at the end and runs into the first break, so that if your machine gives trouble you miss none of the talk.

## 1. The plan of the day

**On the slides.** The facilitator sets out the plan of the day and its two kinds of aim, what you will understand and what you will be able to do. The slides also say what you do not need: no installation, no git, and no GitHub or OSF account. Open the browser lab in a tab while the facilitator talks.

[Open the browser lab](../../cases/housing/lab.qmd){.btn .btn-outline-primary target="_blank"}

## 2. The credibility of social science

**On the slides.** Follow the talk on what social science is for, on false positives and forking paths, and on the evidence from replications and many-analysts studies. It goes on to incentives and questionable research practices, which matter far more than fraud, and to the red-card study, in which twenty-nine teams analysed one dataset, with the estimates that they returned. It then shows why 'replication' names three different operations, set out as a matrix of data against analysis with a quick check on it, and ends on the practices of open research.

## 3. SCORE and Multi100

**On the slides.** The SCORE programme ran three studies, of reproducibility, robustness and replicability, and the slides give the results of each and the finding that the three do not travel together. They then present Multi100 from the position of an analyst inside it: what an analyst received, the two tasks, and how the results were put on a common scale.

## 4. The tools

**On the slides.** The slides cover open-source software, the toolchain, plain-text file formats and what happens when you render, where data and code are archived, the browser lab and the workspace, and what the tools cannot do. An optional run of five slides covers programming languages, editors, packages, version control and licences. Note anything that you might switch to.

## 5. Task 1 – The setup check

[Open the browser lab at Task 1](../../cases/housing/lab.qmd#task-1-setup){.btn .btn-primary target="_blank"}

In the browser lab, wait for the R engine, run the setup cell and check that `audit` has 1,014 rows. The warm-up on the three Rs gives you something to do while the engine downloads. If you have installed the workspace, open its folder in your IDE instead and run `source("R/check_setup.R")` until every line prints OK. The last check fits the reference specification and prints −19.97 percentage points, a number that you meet again later. If you need more time, carry on into the break.

**By the end of the part** you have R running in the browser lab, or in your workspace, with the 1,014 emails of the housing-audit data loaded, and you can tell apart the three operations that go under the single word 'replication'.
